newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan gives strongest economic assessment in 5 yrs.
newsitem.headline: Japan gives strongest economic assessment in 5 yrs.

text.p: In the Japanese government's strongest official assessment of the economy in the last five years, the Economic Planning Agency said Friday that Japan's economy is on the verge of a self-sustaining recovery.
In its annual report, the EPA said "the present state of the economy is close to one where we can say it is recovering autonomously led by private sector demand."
The report said that although the pace of the recovery had slowed after the national sales tax was raised to 5 percent from 3 percent in April, the recovery was not threatened and should continue.
Economists said the report was a fair description of the economy, although some cautioned it had yet to be confirmed by data for capital spending and consumption, due over the next couple of months.
"If capital spending continues to go well, then I think we can say that the recovery has become self-sustaining," said Kenji Arata, an economist at MCM Asia Pacific.
But economists also said the recovery was unlikely to match previous economic recoveries and that growth would be gradual and unspectacular.

A Reuters poll of long-term economic forecasts released on Thursday showed that the average forecast for growth this business year was 1.7 percent, while the 1998/99 business year should see growth of around 2.5 percent.

After years of recession brought on by the bursting of the land and asset price "bubble" of the late 1980s, the economy has spent the most part of the past two years weaning itself away from government efforts to fuel a recovery.
Betting the economy would begin to run under its own steam and with its pockets now empty, the government has embarked on a policy of fiscal tightening, including April's sales tax hike.
Key to the report was the EPA's argument that virtuous business cycles have begun to form.

Starting from the middle of last year, falling inventories led to a pick-up in production across broad sections of industry, which in turn improved employment conditions. In addition, a weakening of the yen, which makes Japanese products cheaper to customers abroad, led to a boom in exports.
"A relatively solid recovery is continuing," Akira Furukawa, the director of the EPA's national economic research bureau, told Reuters Financial Television.
The EPA has been wrong before, however, prematurely stating that a recovery was underway, only to see the economy stall and sputter along.
The report also said the nation's economy has put the worst of the hangover from the bubble years behind it.

While firms in industry and finance may still have balance sheet problems, these problems had slipped from a macro-economic level to a micro-economic level, losing their potential to hinder growth, the report said.

While stressing it did not want to comment on whether or when Japan's interest rates should be raised, the EPA also said that two years had passed since interest rates were cut to rock-bottom levels and firms and individuals should be aware of the risk that interest rates may rise.
Looking forward, it said the key question now was whether the recovery would lead to economic development in the medium to long term.
It added that although the future remained unclear, the economy now had the stamina to embark on drastic reforms and the chance to create free and transparent markets should be seized.
